units: different groups of animals share the same shore without clashing
the web-footed birds search the mud with their bills
these birds leave star-shaped prints in the mud
squat rodents live in the reed belt
these rodents dig tunnels and eat the young stems
their soft coats keep the damp away
the insects hold to the dry part of the slope
the insects feed the animals that fly
the shore reads as three levels stacked one above another
text: Three kinds of creature share the pond's edge, and none of them crowds the others. Web-footed birds work the soft mud, probing the silt with their bills and stamping star-shaped prints wherever they pass. Higher up, where the reeds lie flattened, squat rodents burrow tunnels and gnaw the tender stems down to the pith; their downy coats shed the damp and hold in warmth. On the dry slope the insects take over, smaller, harder to spot, past counting. They spin, they bore, they haul, and they feed everything that flies overhead. Watch long enough and the bank sorts itself into three floors stacked one above another: water, mud, cropped grass. Each floor sets its own food, its own hours, its own quiet. The edge is no single stretch of scenery but a pile of narrow territories, stitched together.

units: the writer holds that public argument has not kept up with tracking methods
counting was first done by eye and written down on paper
colored marks then made it possible to follow one animal
those marks unsettled the species least willing to be approached
shrunken transmitters now record movement without a break
these devices also measure how deep a dive goes and how fast a heart beats
the writer judges that each advance shifts the moral problem instead of settling it
a light device still changes what a bird spends in energy
the writer asks that an outside body approve every fitting
text: Let it be said plainly: watching wild populations has become a different practice, and public argument has not kept pace. At first people counted by eye, notebook in hand, with every bias such a method carries. Then came bands and colored marks, which let a single animal be followed but unsettled the shyest species. Shrunken transmitters came after, reading movement without a break, down to how deep a dive goes and how fast a heart beats. Every technical step has shifted the moral question instead of settling it. A sensor weighs almost nothing, yet it alters how a migrating bird cuts the air and what the flight costs it in energy. My own stand is firm. Nothing should be fitted unless it answers a stated question, unless an outside body has cleared it, and it should come off once the data stops being usable.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who looks after the horses had not aimed for this job
a knee injury pushed her out of her first trade
that injury forces her to move without haste
the fearful animals came close to her before the others did
she names each move aloud before any contact
stubborn animals turn biddable within a season
nearby places send her the animals written off as hopeless
she credits a limit set on her body rather than a gift
she forbids the beginners she trains to move at a run
text: The keeper in charge of the horse stalls never set out to hold that post. A knee injury had ended her work in the harness shop, and the same injury steered her toward the boxes. Because she limped, she moved slowly, and the nervous animals, used to quick hands, came to her before any of the calmer ones did. Out of that forced slowness a method grew. She learned to name each move aloud before her hand reached out, and within a single season the balkiest of them turned biddable. Word spread to the shelters nearby, which began sending her the cases everyone else had given up on. She refuses the word gift. Her advantage, she says, comes from a limit set on her body, and anyone willing to slow down would get the same result. She trains apprentices now, and forbids them to run down the aisles.

units: the reviewer finds the pictures in the film a success
the reviewer faults the narration for handing the animals human motives
that shortcut suggests survival comes from weighing options
the viewer leaves moved but no better informed
the last part of the film runs without narration
those sequences were shot at night with a thermal camera
they follow a pack of wolves crossing a wooded corridor
having no speech makes that sequence truer than the opening of the film
text: Nothing is wrong with the pictures in this wildlife film: the framing holds, the patience shows, every surface comes through with precision. The narration is what lets it down. It hands the animals human motives, the she-wolf decides, the hawk chooses, the colony takes revenge, and that shortcut weakens the case, since it suggests survival comes down to weighing options. You leave moved and none the wiser. The cure was already at hand, and the director found it in the closing stretch: the night footage, caught on a thermal camera, runs almost without a word. A pack crosses a wooded corridor, halts, moves on, and no sentence arrives to tell us what the silence means. All at once the scene is truer than everything before it. The lesson holds for the whole genre. Filming is enough, explaining betrays.

units: the writer writes to someone he knows about two cats
the striped cat was already hanging around behind the workshop
a second cat with ginger fur turned up not long ago
the striped cat barely hunts and sleeps on the warm sheet metal
the ginger cat is thin and eats greedily
the ginger cat keeps its distance from people
the writer tried feeding them in one place from two bowls
the ginger one ate what was in both bowls
the writer is thinking of staggering the meals of the two animals
text: Remember the striped cat that hung around behind the workshop? He has a rival now, and the gap between the two is worth a letter. The striped one barely hunts. He sleeps on the warm sheet metal and waits to be served, and he purrs the moment a door creaks. The newcomer is ginger, thin, ravenous, and will not let anyone within three steps of him. One of them has worked out that people are a supply, the other has them down as a threat. Where one begs, the other steals. I tried feeding them together, two bowls set well apart, and it was a poor idea. The ginger one emptied both, and the striped one stared at me as though I had sold him out. So I will stagger the meals, one at first light and one after dark, and let them settle it. Come by some evening and watch, you will laugh. Write if you want me to keep the ginger one until autumn.

units: a specialist in animal behavior answers the reporter's questions
the subject is the massed flights of birds above river mouths
the specialist puts forward three explanations
living in a crowd lowers the odds that any one bird is taken
the birds find food by watching those that come back full
the flock locates the fish without a leader pointing the way
birds pressed close hold their heat better through the night halts
the specialist denies that these flights have a ranking
each bird matches its speed to whoever flies nearest
text: We put the question of massed bird flights above the river mouths to a specialist in animal behavior. Is there any organization behind those drifting clouds? Her answer came in three parts. Safety comes first: a crowd spreads the risk around, and any single bird stands less chance of being taken while it travels inside a shifting mass. Information comes second: the ones arriving late follow those coming back full, and the whole flock learns where the fish are without any leader pointing the way. Heat comes third, for pressed close through the night halts, the birds lose far less of it. Is there a ranking all the same? She will not have it. What she describes are local rules, each bird matching its speed to whoever flies nearest, and a shape over the whole that nobody ever intended.

units: the herdsman comes to warn before sunrise
he reports that one animal is missing
the neighbor holds that the fog makes any search pointless
the herdsman answers that the animal has been moving badly since the day before
three people set out together to look for the animal
the herdsman explains that the animal follows smells instead of its own kind
the neighbor hears breathing behind some brambles
the animal is found lying down and alive at the foot of the slope
the herdsman carries the animal back on his shoulders
text: Before sunrise the old herdsman knocked at the shutter and said one of the animals had not come in. My neighbor, still in her shawl, told him nobody goes looking for a horned beast in fog, and that waiting would serve better. He answered that it had been limping since the day before and could not have gone far. The three of us set out. On the path he explained he had seen it drift toward the ravine, and that it had the fault of following smells rather than its own kind. Then my neighbor said she could hear breathing, down there, behind the brambles. The herdsman climbed down, pushed the branches apart and called up that she was there, lying still and alive. He carried her back on his shoulders without one word of complaint. Walking home he said only that the next outing would be hers alone, and he laughed under his breath.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: taming reached first for the species that put up with human presence
a herd species already lives inside a ladder of rank
such a species grants an outsider the top place
a solitary territorial species never concedes that place to an outsider
human groups held on to the lines whose young could bear being close
individuals that could not be approached bred poorly behind fences
the sorting therefore happened with no plan behind it
tamed animals show a shorter jaw and drooping ears
these traits show up together because they trace back to the same cells of the embryo
text: Taming did not begin with the most useful of the wild species but with the most tolerant ones. A herd animal already lives inside a ladder of rank, so it will readily grant an outsider the top place, something a solitary, territorial animal never concedes. One consequence follows at once: human groups held on only to the lines whose young could bear being close. The wary ones fled or struck out, and they bred poorly behind fences, so the sorting happened with almost no plan behind it. Build and temper changed together as a result: the jaw shortened, the ears drooped, aggression fell away, adulthood arrived later. Those traits show up as a set because they trace back to the same cells in the embryo. Tameness, then, was never taught to anything at all. It was simply harvested.

units: amphibians leave the woods for the ponds where they hatched
their route often crosses a road
these web-footed animals advance in short hops
they freeze in the glare of headlights
they travel mostly after sunset
a local population can die out within three seasons
one answer is a low fence steering the animals toward a duct
the structure costs a lot but works with nobody watching it
a second answer closes the road on the nights of heaviest migration
both answers call for the usual crossings to have been mapped beforehand
text: When the mild season comes back, amphibians leave the woods for the ponds where they hatched. Their route often crosses a road, and the losses there run high: these web-footed creatures advance in short hops, freeze in the glare of headlights, and travel mostly after sunset, when traffic is still moving fast. A local population can die out within three seasons. Two answers have been tested. The first is a low fence set along the roadside, steering the night travelers toward a duct that runs beneath the surface. The structure costs a great deal, but it works with nobody watching it. The second, far lighter, closes the road on the nights when the migration is heaviest. Both call for the usual crossings to have been mapped beforehand, and only patient watching makes that possible.

units: two young dogs of the same age reached the shelter on the same evening
the first dog is heavy-set and flecked with gray
the first dog puts up with handling and asks for contact
the second dog flinches at noise and comes out only once it is dark
the staff thought the first dog would be taken very fast
it was the second dog that left the shelter first
a family kept her precisely because she stayed out of sight
that family found their home too quiet for a restless animal
the first dog waited until autumn
the manager concludes that the friendliest animal is not the one taken first
text: Nobody would have bet on the pup that hid at the back of its kennel. Two dogs of the same age had been left at the shelter on the same evening, and the staff never tired of comparing them. The first was heavy-set and flecked with gray, and she put up with any handling. She ate everything, slept anywhere, and asked for a hand on her head each time a door opened. The second flinched at the clatter of a bucket and came out of her shelter only once it was dark. The keepers reckoned the first would be gone in a week. It was the second who found a home first. A family chose her exactly because she stayed out of sight, saying a quiet household suited a restless animal badly. The flecked one waited until autumn, passed over by visitors who found her pushy. The manager draws a lesson he keeps repeating: the friendliest animal is not the one who leaves first.
